Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you: and pray for those who persecute and slander you: so that you may be children of your father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise over the good and the bad, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust. <margin>Enemies must be loved.</margin> You reply: "He did not say those things to me. He said them to the apostles: he said them to the perfect." Have you not heard: "so that you may be children of your father"? If you do not desire to be a child of God, the law does not pertain to you. Although not even he is good, who does not wish to be perfect. Take this also: if you do not desire a reward, the commandment is nothing to you. For it follows: "For if you love those <margin>Luke 6</margin> who love you, what reward will you have?" As if he were to say: none. For to do that is not a virtue, but not to do it is a crime. Nothing is owed to either side when like is returned for like. Listen to Paul, the great lawyer and interpreter of Christian laws. <margin>Paul the legal consultant.</margin> Bless those who persecute you: bless, and do not <margin>Romans 12</margin> curse. Rendering to no one evil for evil. If it is possible, as much as lies in you: having peace with all men: not defending yourselves, most dearly beloved: but give place to wrath. For it is written: vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> Lord. But if your enemy is hungry: feed him. If he is thirsty: give him a drink. For in doing this you shall heap coals of fire upon his head. Do not be overcome by evil: but overcome evil with good. What then will happen, you ask, if I nourish another's insolence by my gentleness: and <margin>It befits a Christian to suffer injuries rather than to do them.</margin> by enduring an old injury, I invite a new one? If you can either escape or repel evil without your own evil: no one forbids you from doing so. Otherwise, beware of saying: "it is easier to do it than to suffer it." If you can: amend him, either overwhelming him with benefits or conquering him with mildness. But if not: it is better that one perish than both. It is better that you grow rich with the profit of patience, than that both become evil through mutual retaliation of evil. Therefore, let it be a Christian decree: to contend with all in <margin>The decree of Christianity.</margin> love, mildness, and benefit: but to yield willingly, even to the lowest, in contention, detraction, insult, or injury. "But he is unworthy," you say, "to be benefited, or to be yielded to." Yet you are worthy to do it: Christ is worthy, for whose grace it is done. "I do not wish to harm anyone," they say, "nor will I suffer myself to be harmed." <summary>Erasmus argues that the command to love enemies and endure injuries applies to all Christians, not just the perfect, as it is the requirement for being a child of God. He uses the teachings of Christ and Paul to emphasize overcoming evil with goodness and patience rather than retaliation.</summary>
<keywords>Christian ethics, Sermon on the Mount, St. Paul, patience, forgiveness, non-retaliation, charity, Enchiridion</keywords>
